When something takes a toll, it means it causes gradual damage, harm, or negative effects — slowly wearing something or someone down over time. It always points to a cost or a loss — not a sudden, one-time hit, but a slow, building burden that leaves something worse than it was before.

Think of it this way: imagine filling a bucket with water, one drop at a time. Each drop seems small, but after a while, the bucket overflows. "Take a toll" describes that kind of slow, accumulating damage.
Where the Word "Toll" Comes From

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand the word "toll" first.

A toll is a fee or charge you must pay — usually to use a road, a bridge, or a tunnel. When you drive on a toll road, you pay a price for the privilege of using it.

Now, the idiom borrows this idea metaphorically. When hardship, stress, or time "takes a toll" on you, it is as if life is charging you a price — not in money, but in your health, energy, happiness, relationships, or something else valuable. You are being made to pay without choosing to.

There is also a connection to the phrase "death toll," which means the number of deaths caused by a disaster or war. This reinforces the idea that a "toll" is always about loss — something being taken away.
The Full Grammar Structure

The most complete form of the idiom is:

[Something] takes a toll on [someone/something]

  • The subject (the thing doing the harm) comes first.
  • "Takes a toll" is the verb phrase.
  • "On" connects it to the victim or the thing being damaged.

Examples of the full structure:

  • "Stress takes a toll on your heart."
  • "The bad weather took a toll on the harvest."
  • "Years of smoking have taken a toll on his lungs."

You can also drop the "on" part when the context is already clear:

  • "All this travelling is really starting to take a toll." (The listener understands — it's taking a toll on the speaker.)
The Word "Heavy" and Other Intensifiers

You will very often see adjectives placed before "toll" to show how severe the damage is. These are called intensifiers. The most common ones are:

  • a heavy toll — "The war took a heavy toll on the country." (very serious damage)
  • a terrible toll — "The floods took a terrible toll on the village."
  • a serious toll — "Lack of sleep takes a serious toll on concentration."
  • a significant toll — more formal; used in writing and news.

You can also specify what kind of toll it is by adding a descriptive word:

  • a physical toll — damage to the body
  • an emotional toll — damage to your feelings or mental state
  • a mental toll — damage to your thinking or mental health
  • a financial toll — damage to your money or economy

Examples:

  • "Caring for a sick parent takes an enormous emotional toll."
  • "The injury took a physical toll — he never ran as fast again."
What Kinds of Things "Take a Toll"?

The subject — the thing causing the harm — is almost always a force, situation, condition, or ongoing experience, not usually a single person directly harming another. Common subjects include:

  • Stress: "Chronic stress takes a toll on the immune system."
  • Time: "Time takes a toll on all of us."
  • Weather/climate: "Harsh winters take a toll on old buildings."
  • Work/overwork: "Working 80-hour weeks is taking a toll on her marriage."
  • War/conflict: "The civil war took a heavy toll on the economy."
  • Bad habits: "Years of poor diet have taken a toll on his health."
  • Illness: "The long illness took a toll on the whole family."
Key Characteristics — What Makes This Idiom Special

Understanding these three features will help you use it perfectly every time:

1. The damage is almost always gradual.
This idiom rarely describes something that happened in a single moment. It describes wear and tear — like rust slowly eating metal, not a hammer suddenly breaking it.

  • ✅ "Years of arguing took a toll on their friendship." (gradual)
  • ❌ Using it to describe a single sudden accident would feel unnatural.

2. The effect is always negative.
"Take a toll" is never used to describe something good. It always signals harm, loss, decline, or suffering. You will never hear someone say something took a toll and mean it in a positive way.

3. There is an idea of inevitability.
The phrase often carries a feeling that this damage was hard to avoid — it was the natural consequence of circumstances. It doesn't usually imply blame toward a person; it implies that something difficult simply had a cost.
Tense Forms You Will Encounter

Since the damage is often gradual or ongoing, this idiom appears in many tenses. Here are the most common:

  • Present continuous (happening right now, ongoing):

"The long commute is taking a toll on my energy."

  • Simple past (it happened and is done):

"The recession took a toll on small businesses."

  • Present perfect (it happened in the past and the effects are visible now):

"Years of hard work have taken a toll on his body — he looks exhausted."

  • Future (warning that damage will come):

"If you keep skipping sleep, it will take a toll on your health."
Real-Life Contexts Where You'll Hear It

This idiom is extremely common. You'll find it:

  • In news articles: "The economic crisis has taken a heavy toll on the middle class."
  • In everyday conversation: "I haven't been exercising — honestly, it's taking a toll."
  • In health discussions: "Anxiety takes a serious toll on physical health too."
  • In sports: "The injuries have taken a toll on the team this season."
  • In relationship discussions: "The distance took a toll on their relationship."
Similar Expressions (So You Recognise the Idea Elsewhere)

These phrases carry a similar meaning and are often used in the same situations:

  • "Wear someone/something down" — "The stress wore him down over the years."
  • "Leave its mark on" — "The tragedy left its mark on the whole community."
  • "Catch up with someone" — "Years of unhealthy eating finally caught up with him."
  • "Drain" — "The job drains me emotionally."
  • "Exact a price/cost" — more formal; "The campaign exacted a heavy cost on the party."
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Learners sometimes confuse the spelling and write "toll" as "toil" (which means hard work). They are completely different words. Remember:

  • Toll = a fee, a count of losses, or the damage caused (used in this idiom)
  • Toil = to work very hard for a long time

Also, don't say "take a toll to" — it must always be "take a toll on" when followed by a noun.
One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

"Take a toll" means something is slowly causing damage or harm — like a hidden price that life quietly charges you for going through something difficult.

Once you see this idiom in the wild, you'll immediately recognise it: something is happening, and it is costing someone or something dearly — not all at once, but steadily, over time.
